supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Narrative Review Details Saudi Arabia Pediatric Respiratory Syncytial Virus Burden by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Narrative Review Details Saudi Arabia Pediatric Respiratory Syncytial Virus Burden Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive narrative review published in the Journal of Infection and Public Health demonstrates that respiratory syncytial virus constitutes a major cause of pediatric respiratory morbidity and hospital admissions across Saudi Arabia, concentrating its clinical impact predominantly among young infants during the autumn and winter months. Conducted by researchers Ammar A. Basabrain, Alaa M. Alkinani, Nedaa A. Alabdali, Chu Guat Yeap, and Thamir A. Alandijany, the investigation synthesized observational investigations, hospital-based surveillance reports, molecular genotyping studies, and health-economic models to characterize the pathogen’s epidemiological burden, regional seasonal timing, and emerging prophylactic approaches within the Kingdom. By evaluating decades of published pediatric data alongside recent genomic and post-pandemic surveillance, the authors outlined how viral circulation affects acute healthcare utilization and examined how evolving monoclonal antibodies and maternal immunization regimens might alter future infant disease prevention. To assemble the evidence base, the review team executed two complementary semantic literature searches using the Elicit platform, focusing on pediatric populations aged eighteen years or younger within Saudi Arabia or studies containing extractable Saudi-specific subgroup data. Eligibility criteria required laboratory confirmation via polymerase chain reaction, antigen detection, serology, or viral culture, as well as an established observational, surveillance, systematic review, or meta-analysis study design featuring a sample size of at least ten confirmed cases. Case reports, small case series, and investigations lacking distinguishable pathogen-specific outcomes were excluded from the analysis. The authors manually screened publications, cross-checking extracted clinical settings, observation periods, diagnostic methods, seasonal patterns, and economic parameters directly against primary sources, opting for a narrative synthesis rather than statistical pooling due to substantial heterogeneity in regional study denominators, clinical case selection, and diagnostic protocols. The synthesized prevalence data reveal that respiratory syncytial virus is repeatedly identified across Saudi healthcare centers, though reported detection proportions vary widely depending on study design and patient selection. Across general pediatric respiratory cohorts in tertiary centers, detection proportions commonly ranged between twenty and thirty percent. For example, early surveillance in Riyadh among hospitalized children under five years of age detected the virus in 413 of 1,429 screened children, or 28.9 percent, accounting for 79.1 percent of all virus-positive samples in that cohort. Subsequent cohorts in Riyadh noted detections of 22.4 percent and 26.9 percent in symptomatic pediatric populations. Broader multi-year analyses spanning the Eastern Province observed positive findings in 26.3 percent of 1,279 tested patients, while a retrospective analysis across the Middle East and North Africa region noted a consistent baseline range between 20 percent and 25 percent in Saudi pediatric settings. Marked variations in detection rates were directly linked to clinical severity cohorts and testing denominators rather than genuine geographic boundaries. In selected populations admitted with acute bronchiolitis, detection rates rose substantially; one multi-year bronchiolitis cohort of 417 patients found the virus in 54.9 percent of cases, while another cohort examining 142 tested infants under two years identified positive results in 50.0 percent of screened infants, representing 53.8 percent of virus-positive samples. Conversely, studies examining broad or mixed-age populations with respiratory symptoms reported much lower proportions, including 10.1 percent among 834 tested individuals in Jeddah and 0.14 percent among 5,864 screened individuals in Taif, where influenza A accounted for 71.1 percent of viral detections. The authors emphasized that these contrasting percentages reflect differing clinical thresholds for laboratory testing and varying pediatric age criteria rather than intrinsic regional differences in viral transmission. Across all reviewed epidemiological investigations, young age emerged as the primary determinant of clinical severity and hospitalization. A regional systematic review highlighted that children under twelve months of age accounted for 68.6 percent of all pediatric cases, while a tertiary specialist hospital cohort in Riyadh documented that 77.7 percent of all virus-associated hospital admissions were concentrated in infants during the first six months of life. Although several analyses noted a higher proportion of detections among male infants, such as 59.6 percent in regional surveillance data, age remained the single most consistent demographic indicator of severe lower respiratory tract involvement. In addition to young age, underlying vulnerabilities including prematurity, chronic lung disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease were repeatedly documented among pediatric patients requiring critical-care admission or specialized respiratory support. The review detailed substantial healthcare resource utilization associated with pediatric infections, particularly within inpatient and intensive care units. In an 885-patient tertiary cohort in Riyadh, 60.3 percent of confirmed pediatric patients required hospital admission, with 26.2 percent of those admitted needing intensive care support, 13.1 percent requiring ventilatory assistance, and an observed overall mortality rate of 2.4 percent. In Jazan, among 195 hospitalized cases, 31.8 percent were admitted to intensive care, 40.0 percent received oxygen or ventilatory support, and the mortality rate reached 8.7 percent, with patients in intensive care experiencing a mean hospital stay of 12.13 days compared to 6.24 days for non-intensive care patients. In the Eastern Province, the mean inpatient hospital stay was 6.5 days, while median stays in Riyadh reached six days for ward admissions and five days in intensive care, illustrating prolonged critical-care demands generated by severe cases. Surveillance spanning multiple Saudi provinces demonstrated an established seasonal rhythm, with viral activity concentrating primarily between October and March and reaching peak intensity during December and January. Long-term surveillance in Riyadh documented lowest circulation during the summer months of June through August alongside inverse associations with ambient temperature and positive associations with relative humidity. Southwestern surveillance in Jazan likewise identified peak activity in December with 29.2 percent of cases, followed by January with 22.1 percent. However, the timing of onset and duration showed notable flexibility across individual seasons and regions, with certain cohorts detecting circulation starting as early as August or September and persisting into April, cautioning against the application of rigid, five-month temperate-climate definitions to national prophylaxis administration calendars. The historical seasonal patterns were substantially disrupted during the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by an altered resurgence of pediatric infections. During periods of rigorous non-pharmaceutical interventions and movement restrictions, national viral detection plummeted; in the Eastern Province, no viral infections were detected during the primary pandemic months and the subsequent winter, accompanied by a documented drop in pediatric lower respiratory tract admissions from roughly 400 annually to 201 in 2020. As public health restrictions eased, circulation rebounded with unusual timing, including an off-season August 2021 surge in the Eastern Province and an early resurgence in Riyadh starting in October 2022. Investigators attributed these temporary shifts to an accumulation of susceptible, immunologically naive infants during periods of suppressed viral transmission, though whether seasonal boundaries have permanently shifted remains an active surveillance question. Molecular surveillance from Riyadh, Jeddah, and other centers confirmed the active co-circulation and ongoing evolution of both viral subgroups, RSV-A and RSV-B. Longitudinal tracking showed shifting predominance between subgroups over time; earlier studies in Riyadh and Jeddah documented RSV-A frequencies of 77 percent and 64 percent, respectively, whereas winter surveillance during 2022 and 2023 in Riyadh identified a slight predominance of RSV-B. Genotyping revealed evolutionary transitions, including the replacement of older NA1 strains by ON1 genotypes harboring a 72-nucleotide duplication in the G-protein gene, while RSV-B isolates clustered within the BA lineage carrying a 60-nucleotide duplication. Detailed sequencing of the prefusion fusion protein identified conservation across primary antigenic sites but highlighted eight amino-acid substitutions in RSV-B isolates, including six within antigenic site II, emphasizing the need for continued genomic tracking as monoclonal antibodies targeting these specific epitopes enter broader use. Historically, passive prophylaxis in Saudi Arabia has relied on palivizumab, administered as monthly intramuscular injections throughout the circulation period to high-risk infants with prematurity, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or congenital heart disease. An eight-season study in Riyadh involving 1,704 high-risk infants demonstrated infection rates ranging from 3.9 percent to 9.1 percent across different dosing schedules. Additionally, a local Phase II clinical study in 18 high-risk infants verified the tolerability and pharmacokinetic maintenance of an extended seven-dose regimen tailored for prolonged local transmission periods. However, because palivizumab is restricted to high-risk groups, it leaves the broader infant population unaddressed; in one tertiary bronchiolitis cohort, only 5.6 percent of admitted children had received prophylaxis, underscoring that targeted approaches cannot mitigate overall hospital burden. To evaluate broader infant protection, health economists developed a national decision-analytic model simulating universal administration of nirsevimab, a single-dose long-acting monoclonal antibody. International clinical trials had demonstrated roughly 70 to 80 percent efficacy against medically attended lower respiratory infection and 62 to 83 percent efficacy against hospitalization, with real-world effectiveness reaching 80.7 percent. Assuming 90 percent coverage across a birth cohort, the Saudi model estimated that universal administration could avert approximately 58 percent of hospitalizations, intensive care admissions, and mechanical ventilation events, as well as 53 percent of emergency and primary care visits. The model projected the prevention of 8 of 14 annual infant deaths and reductions in direct respiratory-related healthcare expenditures between 274 million and 343 million Saudi riyals. The authors underscored critical methodological caveats regarding these economic projections, noting that they relied strictly on trial-derived efficacy inputs rather than observed domestic effectiveness or actual vaccine uptake rates. The model evaluated reductions in healthcare resource expenditure without incorporating drug acquisition costs, administrative delivery expenses, comprehensive implementation investments, or local antibody-escape data. Furthermore, while emerging options such as the fixed-dose monoclonal antibody clesrovimab and maternal bivalent prefusion F vaccination demonstrated robust international trial efficacy, no clinical-effectiveness studies have yet been conducted within Saudi Arabian populations. The review concluded that translating emerging immunization tools into national policy will require coordinated surveillance to establish standardized case definitions, determine regional timing, monitor viral antigenic drift, and conduct prospective real-world cost-effectiveness analyses. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Nirsevimab-Resistant RSV-B Variant Detected in Antibody-Naïve Adult with Severe Infection by November 20, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Nirsevimab-Resistant RSV-B Variant Detected in Antibody-Naïve Adult with Severe Infection Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A nirsevimab-resistant respiratory syncytial virus subtype B variant harboring a dominant F:K68Q substitution in the viral fusion protein was identified in a 64-year-old immunocompromised adult hospitalized with severe infection who had never received monoclonal antibody prophylaxis. The case was documented by clinicians and researchers investigating virological determinants of disease severity, demonstrating longitudinal persistence of the resistant strain across sequential respiratory samples collected during hospitalization. The patient was enrolled as part of the ongoing ARF-RSV study, registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT06197152, which is an observational, prospective multicenter cohort conducted across 12 participating hospital centers in France. The primary objective of the cohort investigation is to characterize viral genomic diversity, identify biomarkers linked to respiratory syncytial virus infection severity in adult populations, and validate their potential application in clinical practice. Under the ARF-RSV protocol, adult patients hospitalized for acute respiratory infection with polymerase chain reaction-confirmed viral infection are prospectively evaluated. The study protocol defines severe illness as acute respiratory failure corresponding to a score of six or higher on the World Health Organization ten-point scale at any time during hospitalization, comparing those patients against individuals with mild disease whose scores remain below six. As of June 2026, the multicenter effort had enrolled 117 participants toward a planned recruitment target of 233 patients. The patient described in the report had a recorded medical history of aggressive mantle cell lymphoma undergoing active management, insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension. One week before admission to an intensive care unit, he had received lymphodepletion chemotherapy in preparation for planned chimeric antigen receptor T-cell administration, and he had not received vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus prior to entering the cellular therapy program. Upon admission to the intensive care unit, the patient presented with severe sepsis in the setting of febrile aplasia and a respiratory syndrome that had been evolving for seven days prior to presentation. Clinical management required initial hemodynamic support consistent with septic shock, alongside empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic coverage for a suspected but undocumented concurrent bacterial infection. Hemodynamic failure resolved within a few days, and his planned chimeric antigen receptor T-cell infusion was temporarily suspended before being successfully administered one month later. Diagnostic microbiology confirmed respiratory syncytial virus infection in initial nasopharyngeal material, leading to whole-genome viral sequencing using an amplification framework adapted from the French National Influenza Reference Center protocol. Reference-based genome reconstruction and deep sequencing were performed on two sequential nasopharyngeal swabs collected seven days apart, both achieving complete one-hundred percent genome coverage with high sequencing depth. Genetic analysis determined that the infecting isolate belonged to lineage B.D.E.1 and harbored the F:K68Q substitution within the viral fusion protein in both specimens. In the primary swab, the sequencing run achieved an average coverage depth exceeding 180-fold, detecting the substitution at an allele frequency of 99 percent. The follow-up swab obtained seven days later exhibited an average coverage depth of 170-fold, with the substitution maintained at an allele frequency of 97 percent, confirming the persistence of the resistant variant as the dominant intrahost population over time. Beyond the primary K68Q change, consensus sequencing revealed the presence of R209Q, S190N, and S211N substitutions within the viral fusion protein. Deep sequencing identified no other minority substitutions known to confer resistance within the analyzed fusion protein sequences. The patient had received no prior doses of nirsevimab, establishing that the variant was present in a monoclonal antibody-naïve individual. The F:K68Q substitution has previously been documented to confer high-level resistance to nirsevimab neutralization. In published literature, independent phenotypic neutralization assays by Wilkins and colleagues demonstrated markedly diminished nirsevimab susceptibility in RSV-B carrying K68Q, while deep mutational scanning experiments by Simonich and colleagues independently verified that this specific change strongly impairs antibody neutralization. Global surveillance records from GISAID indicate that the substitution is rare among circulating strains, though historical clusters reported in Kenya in 2017 support its classification as an episodic, naturally occurring polymorphism. The authors highlighted several methodological considerations and study limitations, including the absence of direct phenotypic neutralization assays performed on the patient isolate itself. Additionally, because a seven-day interval elapsed between the onset of respiratory symptoms and hospital admission, investigators could not resolve whether the patient acquired an already-circulating resistant lineage or whether the F:K68Q substitution emerged de novo during replication within the host. The investigators concluded that the documented longitudinal persistence of a resistant viral variant in an antibody-naïve, immunocompromised patient indicates that such strains can persist and potentially transmit within human populations. They noted that prospective genomic surveillance within hospital cohorts remains essential for distinguishing baseline polymorphisms from selective escapes, while respiratory syncytial virus vaccination among immunocompromised groups could provide direct protection and mitigate community dissemination of resistant variants. Beyond the immediate acute presentation, respiratory syncytial virus has increasingly emerged as a major cause of serious clinical morbidity and hospitalization among vulnerable adults, especially individuals living with significant cardiorespiratory comorbidities or severe immunosuppression. Following an acute episode, patients frequently suffer from persistent, debilitating long-term symptoms, underscoring the urgent necessity of expanding proactive viral prevention strategies. In response to this ongoing burden, clinical practice guidelines published by the Infectious Diseases Society of America provide strong recommendations supporting respiratory syncytial virus vaccination for immunocompromised adolescents and adults, specifically highlighting individuals managing hematological malignancies. Concurrently, the recent development and clinical introduction of monoclonal antibodies directed against the viral prefusion fusion protein, including nirsevimab, has marked a substantial therapeutic advance in pediatric medicine by preventing severe disease in infants. Clinicians and researchers anticipate that similar antibody-based strategies targeting the prefusion fusion protein could eventually be utilized to prevent respiratory syncytial virus-related hospital admissions and critical illness in severely immunocompromised adult populations, although emerging alterations within the fusion protein present substantial challenges to this approach. The investigative protocol of the broader prospective cohort incorporates rigorous ethical, temporal, and biological parameters to evaluate disease severity mechanisms. Formal ethical oversight for the investigation was granted by the CPP Sud-Méditerranée I ethics committee on February 3, 2023, under reference number 2022-A02194-39, mandating that written informed consent be obtained from all participating patients or their designated legal representatives prior to data acquisition. Cohort recruitment officially initiated with the inclusion of the first enrolled patient on December 27, 2023. Beyond standard clinical surveillance, the multi-center protocol incorporates an extensive biological evaluation strategy designed to contrast inflammatory and immune pathways between severe and mild disease cohorts. Specifically, researchers perform detailed transcriptomic analyses using peripheral blood and respiratory specimens collected within seventy-two hours of hospital admission. These respiratory materials include routine nasopharyngeal swabs as well as invasive lower respiratory samples, such as bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or tracheal aspirates when clinically obtainable, ensuring comprehensive profiling of host antiviral defenses during early infection. Methodologically, the study authors emphasize that pairing prospective clinical observation with high-resolution genomic surveillance provides crucial clarity regarding viral evolution. In the clinical case, viral genomes were fully assembled and resolved through deep sequencing pipelines, permitting precise quantification of intrahost viral diversity and fine mapping of both dominant alleles and potential minority variants. Establishing whether an observed amino acid change represents an isolated primary polymorphism or an acquired selective escape is critical for interpreting therapeutic efficacy. Because the patient had no recorded prior exposure to monoclonal antibodies, the detection of the dominant F:K68Q variant reinforces the hypothesis that this specific resistant lineage can circulate entirely independently of drug-mediated pressure. Epidemiological evidence from historical respiratory syncytial virus outbreaks, such as previously identified cluster cases in Kenya dating back to 2017, provides concrete historical precedent that K68Q can behave as a naturally occurring polymorphism undergoing episodic expansion in the absence of therapeutic monoclonal antibody selection. The re-emergence of these resistant variants during an era characterized by expanding prophylactic antibody deployment introduces significant epidemiological concerns. When prophylactic agents such as nirsevimab achieve widespread community coverage, existing baseline variants carrying resistance substitutions may encounter selective advantages that facilitate their amplification and subsequent transmission. Within this evolutionary landscape, immunocompromised individuals occupy a uniquely vulnerable position. Because impaired immune systems struggle to achieve swift viral clearance, immunocompromised hosts can serve as substantial anatomical reservoirs supporting prolonged viral replication. This extended duration of replication provides an environment conducive to ongoing intrahost diversification, thereby creating opportunities for resistant variants to stabilize, persist over time, or emerge de novo. Tracking viral kinetics and genomic stability within immunocompromised populations is therefore essential for anticipating broader community transmission dynamics. In discussing the distinctive strengths of their investigation, the authors underscored that conducting the research within a structured, prospective multicenter study framework ensured rigorous sample collection within predefined clinical intervals. Rather than relying on opportunistic retrospective testing, patient evaluations and diagnostic samplings were executed under standardized prospective operational protocols. The systematic acquisition of paired sequential respiratory specimens, separated by a seven-day interval and evaluated via whole-genome deep sequencing, provided definitive molecular proof that the F:K68Q variant maintained absolute intrahost dominance over an extended timeframe. According to the study investigators, this longitudinal persistence of an escape variant carrying documented high-level resistance had not previously been observed or documented in human clinical literature, marking a notable milestone in understanding respiratory syncytial virus evolutionary behavior. Following the relaxation of intervention measures, the traditional winter surge of the virus did not return to its historical timing, shifting instead toward predominant transmission during the summer and autumn months. The study spanned from 2019 to 2025 across four distinct pandemic intervals: a pre-pandemic baseline designated as Phase 1, a strict non-pharmaceutical intervention period designated as Phase 2, a policy transition period designated as Phase 3, and a post-pandemic period designated as Phase 4. Across these intervals, researchers enrolled 108,701 hospitalized children presenting with acute respiratory tract infections, collecting one respiratory specimen from each child for multiplex polymerase chain reaction testing. Multiplex molecular testing demonstrated an overall respiratory syncytial virus positivity rate of 12.37 percent, identifying 13,241 positive cases among 107,015 analyzed children. Infection frequency fluctuated substantially across the four monitoring phases. From a pre-pandemic baseline positivity rate of 17.12 percent, detection declined to 9.41 percent under strict non-pharmaceutical interventions and fell to its lowest point of 5.72 percent during the policy transition period, before rebounding to 13.62 percent in the post-pandemic phase. Surveillance data revealed an enduring disruption in the timing of viral circulation within this subtropical region. Rather than concentrating during the traditional winter months, post-pandemic viral activity peaked in autumn at 22.32 percent positivity and in summer at 16.08 percent positivity. According to the research team, this seasonal displacement from winter to summer and autumn has persisted across approximately three seasons without reverting to pre-pandemic seasonal patterns. Infants younger than one year of age maintained the highest vulnerability to infection throughout the observation period, recording a positivity rate of 22.30 percent. However, the demographic distribution of mixed infections changed considerably after pandemic mitigation measures were lifted. The proportion of co-infections occurring in children younger than three years dropped below 50 percent for the first time, while children aged three to six years accounted for 39.53 percent of all co-infected pediatric patients. The overall rate of respiratory syncytial virus co-detection per child tested measured 1.76 percent before the pandemic, dropped to 0.83 percent during mitigation measures, and increased to 2.12 percent in the post-pandemic period. This post-pandemic frequency marked a 2.55-fold rise over the intervention phase, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 2.24 to 2.90, and a 1.20-fold change compared with pre-pandemic levels, with a 95 percent confidence interval between 0.95 and 1.53. Among mixed viral profiles, co-infections involving human rhinovirus were the most prevalent combination, comprising 76.55 percent of all co-detections. Marked variations emerged among other co-circulating pathogens, particularly Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which experienced severe suppression down to 0.32 percent positivity during mitigation before rebounding to 32.61 percent in the winter. Combined detections of respiratory syncytial virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae recovered from 1.82 percent during the mitigation period to 11.26 percent post-pandemic, whereas human rhinovirus exhibited stable detection and human adenovirus displayed an intermediate response across phases. The investigators noted that the expansion of co-infections into older preschool cohorts might reflect an accumulated immunity debt resulting from prolonged suppression of pathogen exposure. However, the authors explicitly highlighted that the clinical dataset cannot directly evaluate host immunity, emphasizing that confirmation of this hypothesis requires dedicated serological surveillance and birth-cohort studies. In their final assessment, the researchers concluded that COVID-19 mitigation measures altered the epidemiological dynamics of respiratory syncytial virus and co-circulating respiratory pathogens in hospitalized children. Given the persistent changes in seasonal circulation and pathogen co-infections, the authors underscored that ongoing molecular surveillance and age-tailored prevention strategies are essential to manage the re-emerging disease burden. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Surveillance in Bangkok Reveals Influenza and Rhinovirus Dominated 2025 Respiratory Infections by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Surveillance in Bangkok Reveals Influenza and Rhinovirus Dominated 2025 Respiratory Infections Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective surveillance investigation conducted across 2025 in Bangkok, Thailand, identified respiratory viruses in 61.1 percent of patients evaluated for acute respiratory infections. Analyzing 4,697 nasopharyngeal specimens from individuals presenting with acute respiratory symptoms at Bangpakok 9 International Hospital, investigators identified 2,871 positive samples containing 3,151 viral detections. Influenza virus was the predominant pathogen, registering an overall detection rate of 22.2 percent across all tested samples. Human rhinovirus represented the second most frequent agent at 16.6 percent, while SARS-CoV-2 accounted for 9.9 percent of cases. Single-pathogen detections constituted 55.4 percent of samples, whereas multivirus coinfections were confirmed in 5.7 percent of patients. Screening eight viral targets across twelve months established an empirical baseline of viral transmission across patients ranging from one month to 97 years old. Acute respiratory infections represent an enduring public health burden, causing substantial hospitalizations and mortality across all age groups, particularly young children and the elderly. Pathogen diversity is extensive, involving influenza virus, human rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, SARS-CoV-2, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human coronavirus, and human adenovirus. Infection severity depends on pathogen type, coinfections, age, and underlying comorbidities. In tropical settings like Thailand, climatic and geographic factors create circulation dynamics that differ markedly from temperate zones, where infections peak primarily during winter. Tropical transmission frequently exhibits prolonged activity, multiple annual peaks, or virus-specific patterns. Global pandemic disruptions altered viral circulation, shifting seasonal onset and reducing natural exposure. The subsequent resurgence of respiratory infections was driven by declining population immunity and lower vaccine uptake, creating an immunity debt that heightened susceptibility following the lifting of pandemic restrictions. Conducted as a retrospective cohort study, the surveillance evaluated patients who sought medical care for acute respiratory infections at Bangpakok 9 Hospital between January and December 2025. Eligible patients met clinical criteria requiring a measured fever of at least 38 degrees Celsius combined with cough, sore throat, or both symptoms. To avoid duplicate sampling, specimens obtained from the same individual within a 14-day interval or during follow-up visits were excluded. Nasopharyngeal swabs were transported to the Center of Excellence in Clinical Virology at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital for diagnostic testing. Ethical approval was granted by the Institutional Review Board of the Faculty of Medicine at Chulalongkorn University under IRB number 0977/67, adhering to the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice standards. The ethics committee waived individual informed consent because of the noninterventional, retrospective design, and hospital administration formally authorized dataset utilization. Demographic analysis of the 4,697 participants revealed a mean age of 25.3 years with a standard deviation of 23.3 years, spanning from one month to 97 years. Females comprised 54.2 percent of the cohort with 2,547 individuals, while males accounted for 45.8 percent with 2,150 individuals. Adults aged 19 to 60 years formed the largest demographic group, representing 37.9 percent with 1,782 patients. School-aged children aged 6 to 12 years made up 20.6 percent with 965 individuals, followed by preschool children aged 3 to 5 years at 13.5 percent with 632 individuals, infants aged 0 to 2 years at 11.5 percent with 540 individuals, and older adults over 60 years at 10.1 percent with 476 individuals. Adolescents aged 13 to 18 years constituted the smallest age group at 6.4 percent with 302 patients. This broad age distribution allowed researchers to characterize age-specific pathogen susceptibility across distinct developmental categories. Viral identification was performed using automated extraction of nucleic acids from 200 microliters of clinical specimen on a magLEAD 12gC platform, resulting in a 50-microliter elution. Real-time RT-PCR assays targeted specific genetic regions: the matrix gene for influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus, the 5 prime untranslated region for human rhinovirus, the N1 and N2 nucleocapsid genes for SARS-CoV-2, the hemagglutinin-neuraminidase gene for human parainfluenza virus, the fusion gene for human metapneumovirus, the ORF1ab gene for human coronavirus, and the hexon gene for human adenovirus. Amplification of RNA viruses was executed using the SensiFAST Probe No-ROX One-Step Kit with reverse transcription at 42 degrees Celsius for 20 minutes, activation at 95 degrees Celsius for 3 minutes, and 45 cycles of denaturation and annealing. Human adenovirus assays omitted reverse transcriptase. Internal control testing targeted glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and a cycle threshold of 38 or lower defined positive samples. Statistical analyses structured the surveillance timeline into epidemiological weeks and three distinct climate seasons: the warm season from March to May, the rainy season from June to October, and the cold season spanning January through February and November through December. Because weekly sample volumes were low in certain age cohorts, data were aggregated monthly for age-specific positivity analyses. Chi-square and Fisher exact tests compared detection rates across age groups and evaluated shifts between the 2025 cohort and 2024 surveillance figures. Analyses were performed in IBM SPSS Statistics version 23.0, with visualizations generated in R software version 4.5.1, using a significance threshold of p less than 0.05. Beyond influenza, rhinovirus, and SARS-CoV-2, overall detection rates were 4.7 percent for respiratory syncytial virus, 4.6 percent for human parainfluenza virus, 4.0 percent for human metapneumovirus, 3.9 percent for human coronavirus, and 1.2 percent for human adenovirus. Detailed investigation of coinfection patterns demonstrated that human rhinovirus served as a primary contributor to multiple-pathogen infections among ARI patients. Among the 267 confirmed multivirus cases, UpSet plot analysis revealed that dual infections most frequently involved human rhinovirus combined with other circulating respiratory agents. Specifically, dual infections occurred between human rhinovirus and influenza virus in 58 patients, human rhinovirus and respiratory syncytial virus in 29 patients, and human rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 in 21 patients. In addition, 12 discrete cases of triple viral infection were identified, most frequently involving human rhinovirus, human coronavirus, or both in combination with other pathogens. These findings indicate that while rhinovirus frequently co-circulates and co-infects with other common respiratory pathogens, single-virus detections remained the dominant manifestation of viral illness, accounting for 2,604 cases, or 55.4 percent of the total tested population. Seasonal tracking of viral activity demonstrated distinct circulation trajectories across the study year. Influenza virus exhibited a bimodal pattern featuring two discrete peaks: a smaller rise during the cool season between January and March with weekly positivity spanning 6.0 percent to 25.7 percent, and a pronounced surge during the rainy season from July to December ranging from 13.5 percent to 52.8 percent, peaking in September. Human rhinovirus circulated continuously throughout the year with weekly positivity rates between 3.5 percent and 29.5 percent. Respiratory syncytial virus and human metapneumovirus were detected predominantly during the rainy season between July and September, sharing concurrent peaks in August. Conversely, SARS-CoV-2 activity surged during the warm season, reaching its highest positivity in May between 42.2 percent and 48.6 percent. Human parainfluenza virus, human coronavirus, and human adenovirus were detected more frequently in cooler months, though their overall prevalence remained comparatively low. Analysis across age cohorts revealed distinct seasonal timing and positivity levels. Overall viral detection across all age groups showed two distinct peaks between May and June and between September and November. Young children aged 0 to 2 years and 3 to 5 years exhibited prolonged viral activity from May to November, with peak positivity occurring in May and September. School-aged children showed peaks in May and September, while adolescents peaked in June and September. In adults aged 19 to 60 years and older adults over 60 years, viral detection was highest in May. Overall positivity was 69.6 percent in preschool children, 66.2 percent in school-aged children, 65.9 percent in infants, 62.6 percent in adolescents, 57.2 percent in adults, and 47.7 percent in older adults. Multivirus coinfections were most frequent in preschool children at 11.7 percent, followed by school-aged children at 8.3 percent and infants at 7.2 percent. Pathogen distribution differed significantly across demographic groups. Human rhinovirus predominated in infants and preschool children, whereas influenza virus dominated school-aged children and adolescents. Influenza virus was detected at a significantly higher rate among adolescents aged 13 to 18 years than in any other age group. In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 was most frequently detected in adults aged 19 to 60 years and older adults over 60 years, representing the leading viral agents in mature cohorts. Human rhinovirus, human parainfluenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and human coronavirus were detected at significantly higher rates in infants aged 0 to 2 years, whereas human adenovirus and human metapneumovirus were most commonly found in preschool children aged 3 to 5 years. Waning maternal antibodies and high reinfection rates drive high pediatric respiratory syncytial virus burdens, while close classroom contact and indoor exposure foster elevated influenza transmission in school-aged children. Comparing 2025 data to the 2024 cohort revealed substantial shifts in viral epidemiology. Influenza virus, human rhinovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus exhibited significant resurgences with higher positivity rates in 2025. Conversely, SARS-CoV-2 and human adenovirus declined significantly, while human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, and human coronavirus maintained stable detection rates. Peak timing also shifted: SARS-CoV-2 peaked in May rather than April, while influenza’s primary peak moved from July to September with prolonged circulation. Seasonality in Thailand differed from regional neighbors within the intertropical belt: Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar show single influenza peaks, while Malaysia and Vietnam demonstrate year-round activity. Characterizing these patterns supports optimized timing for influenza vaccination campaigns and respiratory syncytial virus interventions, such as maternal vaccines and monoclonal antibodies like nirsevimab, palivizumab, and clesrovimab. However, limitations include the single-center hospital design in Bangkok, a one-year timeframe, absence of bacterial testing, lack of influenza strain subtyping, and absence of clinical outcome data. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health RSV Hospitalizations Rose in Second Year Following Infant Nirsevimab Immunization by November 21, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 RSV Hospitalizations Rose in Second Year Following Infant Nirsevimab Immunization Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Hospital admission rates for respiratory syncytial virus rose significantly during children’s second season of life compared with their initial protection period following nirsevimab immunization, according to a two-year follow-up study published in Frontiers in Public Health. In the adjusted, self-controlled analysis, hospitalization rates during the second RSV season were 7.99 times higher than during the antibody’s period of effectiveness, with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 5.80 to 11.02. Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody developed to protect infants against respiratory syncytial virus and has demonstrated effectiveness in preventing hospitalizations throughout their first RSV season. Nevertheless, questions regarding long-term effects have persisted among researchers. While prior long-term studies indicated no significant differences in second-season events between immunized and non-immunized infants, the trajectory of protection across subsequent seasons required further evaluation. To assess these patterns over time, investigators conducted a self-controlled case series tracking hospital admissions for infants born between April 1, 2023, and March 31, 2024. The study evaluated health outcomes across an observation window extending from October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2025, specifically comparing events between consecutive RSV seasons for children who received nirsevimab during their first season. Discover more Save on Rx Find Lung Care Track Biotech Find Vaccines respiratory syncytial virus The analysis examined a total of 1,152 RSV-associated hospitalizations involving 1,128 participants. Crude observational data demonstrated that admissions among immunized participants increased by 3.42 times during the second RSV season, rising from 147 cases to 503 cases, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 2.84 to 4.14. Furthermore, after accounting for age during peak transmission periods, the risk of hospitalization in the second season remained 4.31 to 12.53 times higher than during the initial period of nirsevimab protection. Admissions to pediatric intensive care units also demonstrated a numerical increase of 2.14-fold, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.87 to 5.30. However, the authors noted that this difference was not statistically significant, pointing out that low statistical power limited the conclusiveness of findings for intensive care admissions. Ultimately, the researchers observed no lingering protective effect or residual efficacy from nirsevimab during the second RSV season. Although baseline risk for RSV hospitalization typically declines with advancing age, this age-related reduction did not prevent an increased disease burden during the second year of life in the cohort. The authors concluded that because these observations contradict earlier evidence, current preventive measures and public health policies warrant reevaluation. Send Close Immunology / Vaccination Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print NOVEMBER 21, 2026 IDWeek 2026 Pfizer’s 25-Valent Pneumococcal Vaccine Candidate Shows Strong Immune Responses in Infants By Ethan Covey An investigational 25-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (25vPnC) elicited robust immune responses against all 25 targeted serotypes in infants, including five additional serotypes not covered by the currently available 20-valent vaccine, according to phase 2 findings presented at IDWeek 2026, in Washington, D.C. Source: Adobe. The vaccine candidate, PF-07872412, which has been developed by Pfizer, also produced substantially higher antibody responses against serotype 3 compared with Prevnar 20 (PCV20; Pfizer), while demonstrating a comparable safety and tolerability profile. Related Content Infant Formula Device Linked to Legionnaires Disease Case Legionnaires disease was identified in an immunocompromised infant who had recently consumed powdered formula ... RSV-B Lineage Emerges as Standout in Severe Pediatric Disease Young children infected with certain respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) subgroup B lineages experienced greater ... Many Children Exposed to Hepatitis B at Home Are Unvaccinated, Study Finds More than 6% of newborns living in households with hepatitis B (HBV)-positive contacts are not vaccinated against ... The phase 2 study evaluated a four-dose series of 25vPnC compared with PCV20 in healthy infants. Immune responses were assessed one month after the third and fourth doses. Investigators reported robust responses against all 25 serotypes, including the five additional serotypes: 15A, 23A, 23B, 24F, and 35B. Functional antibody responses, measured using an opsonophagocytic activity assay, were also observed against all 25 targeted serotypes one month after the fourth dose. Of particular interest were the findings for serotype 3, which has historically presented challenges for pneumococcal vaccine development. The investigational vaccine uses next-generation technology designed to enhance immune responses against this serotype. Compared with PCV20, 25vPnC generated serotype 3 antibody geometric mean concentrations that were 8.8-fold higher one month after the third dose and approximately 15-fold higher one month after the fourth dose. “The most important finding is the robust immune response to serotype 3,” said study investigator Michael J. Smith, MD, MSCE, a professor of pediatrics and the chief of pediatric infectious diseases at Duke University Medical Center, in Durham, North Carolina. Dr. Smith also highlighted the potential significance of the additional serotypes, particularly 35B, which he identified as a leading cause of meningitis, and 23B, which has been associated with bacteremia. Regarding safety, rates of local reactions, systemic events, and adverse events were similar between the two vaccine groups. No related serious adverse events were identified during the study. Dr. Smith said the findings suggest that the investigational vaccine could broaden serotype coverage without compromising immune responses against serotypes shared with PCV20, while maintaining a similar safety profile. “These data support the phase 3 study that is underway and will provide additional confirmatory data in a larger group of children,” he said. Pfizer estimates that the 25 serotypes targeted by the vaccine candidate are collectively responsible for approximately 84% of invasive pneumococcal disease cases among U.S. children younger than 5 years of age. Three phase 3 studies evaluating 25vPnC began earlier in 2026, with up to 6,830 participants expected to be randomized to receive the investigational vaccine or PCV20. “We’ll continue to closely monitor serotype 3 in our late-stage studies, as we’ve already seen a strong immunologic starting point,” a Pfizer spokesperson told Infectious Disease Special Edition. If successful, the phase 3 program could support development of a vaccine offering broader serotype coverage for pediatric pneumococcal disease prevention. Pfizer funded the study of its vaccine candidate. NEWS COMMUNITY Arts – Entertainment Business Education Health In Memoriam ENVIRONMENT Gardening/Agriculture Orca Sustainability Tourism GOVERNMENT Ferries Land Use Public Safety Sheriff’s Report OPINION Column As the Paradigm Shifts Midnight Mutterings Occam’s Razor Editorial Guest Opinion Letters $UPPORT $UBSCRIBE Previous Next Public Health Hot Topic | Vaccinate before holiday gatherings By Community|2026-11-20T12:00:40-08:00November 20th, 2026|0 Comments View Larger Image   FacebookEmailCopy LinkXShare/Bookmark Public health tips for a happy and healthy holiday season ||| FROM SAN JUAN COUNTY COMMUNICATIONS ||| Each year, respiratory illnesses are responsible for millions of illnesses and thousands of hospitalizations and deaths in the United States. In addition to the virus that causes influenza (flu), there are many other types of respiratory viruses, including COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The good news is there are actions you can take to help protect yourself and others from health risks caused by respiratory viruses. Cases usually rise in the weeks following holiday gatherings, so if you haven’t gotten your updated vaccines yet, now is a great time! Getting your updated vaccines before holiday gatherings will shield you against the worst of these illnesses. If you or a loved one tests positive for the flu or COVID-19, seeking early medical treatment to get prescription antivirals can reduce the severity of the illness. Staying up to date on flu, COVID-19, and RSV vaccines (for those who are eligible) is an important step to take to protect yourself and those around you. For adults who have insurance, please reach out to your primary health care provider to see if they have these vaccines available for you. You may also contact your local pharmacy to see if they have availability: Friday Harbor Drug on San Juan Island can be reached by calling (360) 378-4421 – you can also schedule a vaccine appointment on their website (if vaccine is available) Ray’s Pharmacy in Eastsound can be reached by calling (360) 376-2230 – you can also schedule a vaccine appointment on their website (if vaccine is available) Lopez Island Pharmacy on Lopez Island can be reached by calling (360) 468-2616 – you can also schedule a vaccine appointment on their website (if vaccine is available) Alternatively, you may be able to schedule a vaccine appointment at an off-island pharmacy. San Juan County Health & Community Services (HCS) has appointments for children through the age of 18 years and uninsured adults available for COVID-19 and influenza (flu) vaccines at our regularly scheduled clinics on Lopez, Orcas, and San Juan Islands. As a friendly reminder, HCS can only vaccinate children through the age of 18 years and adults who do not have insurance. You can schedule your appointment through our website or over the phone at 360-378-4474. HCS has a limited amount of adult and pediatric RSV vaccines. For infants and some young children, and for adults without insurance, please call our office at 360-378-4474 or check our website to inquire about RSV vaccine availability. For those adults who have insurance, please reach out to your primary health care provider to see if they have RSV vaccines available for you. You may also contact your local pharmacy to see if they have availability. Preventing Respiratory Illness The best protection against respiratory illnesses is vaccination. Vaccines can prevent the worst symptoms and help keep you out of the hospital if you do become sick. If you have questions about any of the vaccines that can help prevent respiratory illness, please don’t hesitate to reach out and speak with one of our public health nurses. They are always happy to talk with you and answer any questions you may have. Take these actions to keep you and your family safe from respiratory illnesses like influenza, COVID-19, and RSV: Get vaccinated, if possible. Vaccines are your best defense against respiratory illnesses. Some people who get vaccines may still get sick. However, vaccines help reduce the severity of your illness. It will also lower the chance of hospitalization and death. Stay home when you are sick. If you have any of the following symptoms, stay home until you feel better: fever, sore throat, cough, sneezing, headache, nausea and/or vomiting, and diarrhea. Consider masking. If you must go out while you are sick or if you are visiting a vulnerable family member, consider wearing a well-fitting mask to protect those around you. People are considered vulnerable if they are under six months old or over sixty years old or someone who is likely to become severely ill with an illness that seems mild to others. Cover your cough or sneeze. Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or inside of your elbow when you cough or sneeze. Put your used tissue in the waste basket and wash your hands right away. Wash your hands regularly. Use soap and water. If there is no soap available, use an alcohol-based hand sanitizer. Clean and disinfect surfaces that may be contaminated with viruses. Take antiviral drugs if your doctor prescribes them. Healthy Living Colorado COVID Hospital Admissions Jump 50% in a Week as RSV Admissions More Than Double, Mostly in Children Published Nov 20, 2026 12:01 AM EST By Cole Mercer ALAIN JOCARD | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on WhatsApp Colorado hospitals admitted 87 people with COVID-19 in the week ending Nov. 14, up from 58 the week before, a jump of about 50%. In the same week, RSV admissions rose from 6 to 15, and 11 of those patients were children, according to Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) data reported by Kiowa County Press. Flu has drawn most of the attention this fall, with 157 admissions in the same week. But the newest numbers show two more viruses starting to climb as Colorado families prepare for Thanksgiving gatherings. For households, that means more than one virus to plan around. Older adults face the biggest COVID risk, while babies face the biggest RSV risk, and both groups often end up at the same holiday table. A Sharp Weekly Rise After Weeks of Flat COVID Numbers Weekly COVID admissions had stayed between 37 and 58 since early October, which makes the jump to 87 stand out. The count is still far below the same week in 2023, when 344 people were admitted, and not far above the 49 admitted in the same week last season. Other measures mostly moved the same way. COVID accounted for 0.6% of emergency department visits, up from 0.43%. Colorado's wastewater level rose from low to moderate in the week ending Nov. 7, according to CDC ratings cited in the report. Test positivity, however, dipped slightly, to 4.4% from 5%. One week of data does not make a trend. Weekly hospital counts can bounce, and the state's next updates will show whether the rise continues. Nationally, COVID activity remains low, according to the CDC's respiratory illness data, though the national wastewater level is moderate and highest in the West. Older adults carry most of the COVID burden. Of 210 COVID admissions in October with age data, 125 were people 65 and older. Infants younger than 6 months had the highest admission rate of any age group, though that reflected just seven babies. Colorado recorded nine COVID deaths in October, compared with a peak of 43 last January. RSV Rises Early Among Young Children RSV admissions more than doubled in one week, from 6 to 15, according to data from the state's viral respiratory report. Those numbers are small, but the timing matters. Last season, RSV admissions in Colorado did not peak until the week ending Feb. 28, which suggests this season's rise may only be beginning. RSV usually causes a cold in older children and adults. In babies, it can inflame the small airways and make breathing hard. RSV "is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S.," according to the CDC's guidance on protecting infants. Prevention tools are newer than many parents realize. Babies can be protected either by a maternal vaccine given during weeks 32 to 36 of pregnancy or by an antibody shot recommended for infants younger than 8 months whose mothers did not get the vaccine. Most babies need only one of the two. Some higher-risk children ages 8 to 19 months can get an antibody dose for a second season. Flu Still Leads, and Forecasts Point Higher Flu remains the biggest of the three by a wide margin. Colorado has recorded 689 flu hospitalizations since Oct. 4, compared with 107 at this point last season, and nearly all subtyped cases have been H1N1. MedicalDaily earlier reported on Colorado's flu numbers running far ahead of last year's pace. Nationally, CDC forecasts in its weekly influenza surveillance report predict a likely increase in flu hospital admissions through the week ending Nov. 28. That is a forecast, not a certainty. The forecast suggests hospitals may handle several viruses at once in the coming weeks. One measure is running lower than last year: Colorado has reported 19 COVID outbreaks in nursing homes and other residential care facilities since Oct. 4, compared with 36 at the same point last year. The overlap matters most for people with chronic conditions. An older adult with heart failure or a toddler with asthma can get sicker from any of these viruses. It also matters for smaller hospitals, where pediatric beds are limited and very sick children may need transfer to a larger center. Protection Steps Before Holiday Gatherings The CDC recommends the 2026-27 COVID vaccine for adults 18 and older. For children and teens, it is recommended for those with moderately or severely weakened immune systems, and others may get it after talking with a clinician. In September, Colorado reissued a statewide standing order that lets pharmacists give COVID vaccines without a prescription. The RSV vaccine is recommended as a single dose, not yearly, for everyone 75 and older and for adults 50 to 74 at higher risk. Parents of babies younger than 8 months can ask a pediatrician about the antibody shot, which most insurance covers. Children eligible for the Vaccines for Children program can get it at no cost. Anyone with fever, cough, or a sore throat should skip gatherings if possible, especially those that include newborns or frail relatives. Prescription antivirals for COVID and flu work best when started early, so older adults and people with chronic illness should call a clinician quickly if symptoms begin. Parents should seek urgent care for a baby who is breathing fast, pulling in at the ribs, grunting, feeding poorly, or having fewer wet diapers. Bluish lips, pauses in breathing, or extreme sleepiness need a 911 call. MedicalDaily will report whether COVID and RSV admissions keep rising alongside flu. Read more Montana Flu Hospitalizations Reach 96 With Three Deaths This Season, Up From Four Hospitalizations a Year Ago Flu Makes Up Nearly Twice Last Year's Share of Alabama ER Visits as Thanksgiving Gatherings Approach Riverside County Flu Deaths Reach Two as Activity Holds at Very High and Only 15.5% of Residents Vaccinated Oklahoma Reports First Child Flu Death of 2026–27 Season as Activity Climbs Early in OKC and Tulsa Key Questions Answered How much did COVID admissions rise in Colorado? From 58 to 87 in the week ending Nov. 14, an increase of about 50%. How many RSV patients were children? 11 of the 15 RSV admissions in the week ending Nov. 14. Is this a surge? Not yet. One week of data can bounce, and COVID admissions remain far below the 344 recorded in the same week of 2023. Who faces the highest COVID risk? Adults 65 and older made up most October admissions, and infants younger than 6 months had the highest admission rate. How can babies be protected from RSV? Through a maternal vaccine during pregnancy or an antibody shot for infants younger than 8 months. Most babies need only one. When should parents seek urgent care? For fast or labored breathing, poor feeding, fewer wet diapers, bluish lips, or extreme sleepiness. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Comorbid Adults Aged 60 to 74 Face Severe RSV Burden in England by November 19, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Comorbid Adults Aged 60 to 74 Face Severe RSV Burden in England Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A population-based retrospective cohort study evaluating secondary and primary care records across England reveals that adults aged 60 to 74 hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus who present with chronic medical conditions face severe healthcare utilization that is equal to or numerically higher than the burden experienced by individuals aged 75 and older. Respiratory syncytial virus, commonly designated as RSV, represents a substantial cause of acute lower and upper respiratory tract disease among adults, often driving disease progression that exacerbates preexisting vulnerabilities, increases intensive care requirements, and elevates mortality risks. Although preventative adult vaccination strategies in the United Kingdom have historically focused primarily on older chronological age brackets, epidemiological data detailing granular resource use across comorbid younger subsets has remained scarce. The descriptive research published in Infectious Diseases and Therapy establishes that while overall mortality rates remain elevated among the most elderly cohort, critical care admissions and extended hospital stays heavily affect comorbid patients aged 60 to 74 years. To rigorously examine healthcare resource utilization, baseline characteristics, and mortality over time, the investigative team linked longitudinal electronic health records from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Aurum database to secondary care datasets, including Hospital Episode Statistics Admitted Patient Care and Outpatient records, alongside Office for National Statistics mortality registries and the English Index of Multiple Deprivation. The observational indexing framework examined adult patients aged 60 years and older who were admitted to National Health Service hospital facilities in England between October 1, 2014, and March 31, 2019. This multi-year study window was explicitly chosen to span five complete and continuous pre-pandemic respiratory virus seasons while avoiding the disruptive confounding effects of the coronavirus disease pandemic on diagnostic testing priorities, respiratory pathogen transmission, and general healthcare delivery pathways. Within this framework, an episode-level analytical structure was established where each clinical RSV episode followed eligible patients for a full 90 days after an initial index diagnosis code. Discover more Respiratory Syncytial Virus Respiratory syncytial virus Check Symptoms The study protocol instituted two distinct operational case definitions to account for established diagnostic testing realities in secondary care settings, dividing episodes into an RSV-specific category and an RSV-possible category. The RSV-specific case definition required recorded diagnostic codes that specifically identified laboratory-confirmed or physician-coded RSV infection in hospital inpatient records or linked general practice files, including episodes where a possible diagnosis was followed by an explicit RSV-specific code within 14 days. In contrast, the RSV-possible definition captured hospitalizations coded for generalized acute lower respiratory tract infections where other causative pathogens were systematically excluded. This broader definition captured suspected but unconfirmed viral episodes, addressing historical under-testing among adult inpatients where diagnostic testing is infrequently requested, testing sensitivities range from 64 percent to 83 percent for rapid antigen and direct fluorescent antibody methods compared with multiplex polymerase chain reaction testing, and targeted antiviral therapies are unavailable. Discover more Find Treatments respiratory virus Find Lung Care respiratory syncytial virus Across the entire five-season indexing window, the investigators identified 97,712 hospitalized episodes among 89,138 unique individuals aged 60 years and older who met all continuous general practice registration and record-linkage quality criteria. Within this aggregate population, 785 episodes, representing approximately 0.8 percent of all episodes, met the rigorous RSV-specific case definition, comprising 338 episodes among patients aged 60 to 74 years and 447 episodes among individuals aged 75 years and older. The remaining 96,897 episodes fell under the RSV-possible case definition, reflecting 25,645 episodes among individuals aged 60 to 74 years and 71,252 episodes among adults aged 75 years and older. Demographic analyses revealed that among the 338 RSV-specific episodes in the 60-to-74 age group, the mean age was 67.4 years, 55.6 percent were female, 88.2 percent were of White ethnicity, and nearly half resided in the most socioeconomically deprived quintiles according to national deprivation indices. Baseline clinical assessments demonstrated high rates of underlying long-term chronic illness among patients aged 60 to 74 hospitalized with RSV-specific infection. Cardiovascular disease was present in 60.4 percent of these younger episodes, chronic respiratory conditions were recorded in 58.3 percent, and 19.2 percent were immunocompromised, with approximately 80 percent categorized as current or former tobacco smokers. The mean Quan-Charlson Comorbidity Index score was 2.5 among patients aged 60 to 74 years compared with 2.9 among those aged 75 years and older. Furthermore, 93.8 percent of RSV-specific episodes in the 60-to-74 age bracket occurred during the defined seasonal peak between October and March, whereas only 61.0 percent of RSV-possible episodes aligned with this seasonal timeframe, highlighting the preferential clinical deployment of diagnostic testing panels during the winter months. Analyses of secondary care resource consumption uncovered striking variations in hospital bed utilization and high-dependency management between the age cohorts. In the RSV-specific cohort, the median cumulative general inpatient length of stay across the 90-day post-index window was 10.00 days for adults aged 75 years and older, with an interquartile range of 6.00 to 22.00 days. By comparison, individuals aged 60 to 74 with specific comorbid conditions exhibited equal or higher cumulative general hospital lengths of stay, reaching a median of 11.50 days with an interquartile range of 7.00 to 26.00 days among immunocompromised individuals. Inpatient readmissions within 30 days following hospital discharge were also notably prevalent, peaking at 9.2 percent among immunocompromised patients in the 60-to-74 age group, compared with consistently lower readmission proportions in other evaluated subsets. Critical care requirements revealed an even more pronounced divergence between age groups, as patients aged 60 to 74 years were substantially more likely to be admitted to high dependency or intensive care units. In the RSV-specific definition, 18.1 percent of patients aged 60 to 74 years required critical care admission, compared with only 5.03 percent of patients aged 75 years and older. When stratified by underlying conditions, critical care admission rates among comorbid patients aged 60 to 74 ranged from 13.85 percent to 22.34 percent, peaking among those with chronic respiratory conditions, who also experienced a median critical care length of stay of 9.0 days versus 6.0 days in the older age group. Advanced supportive interventions, including non-invasive ventilation, continuous positive airway pressure, invasive mechanical ventilation, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, were similarly utilized at higher rates across all comorbid subgroups aged 60 to 74 years. Outside of hospital inpatient wards, healthcare utilization remained consistently intensive throughout primary care and ambulatory specialty environments. Across all age brackets and comorbidity groups, approximately 80 percent of RSV-specific episodes included at least one general practice or primary care nursing consultation during the 90-day observation window, with the sole exception of immunocompromised patients aged 60 to 74 years, who recorded a consultation rate of 61.5 percent. Outpatient specialist appointments were attended by 47.9 percent of patients aged 60 to 74 years compared with 34.6 percent of those aged 75 and older. Furthermore, primary care prescription rates were substantial: over 50 percent of patients across groups were prescribed antibiotics despite the viral etiology of RSV, reaching 72.7 percent among immunocompromised younger adults, while bronchodilators were prescribed in 76.0 percent of younger patients with underlying chronic respiratory conditions. Evaluation of mortality outcomes demonstrated that fatal events were most concentrated among the oldest demographic group, establishing an important contrast with critical care admission trends. Over the 90-day episode period, the all-cause case fatality rate among RSV-specific cases was 19.3 percent in adults aged 75 years and older, with an RSV-related case fatality rate of 10.3 percent. Among patients aged 60 to 74 years, all-cause and RSV-related case fatality rates were 16.6 percent and 6.5 percent, respectively, with figures of 14.2 percent and 5.1 percent among those with chronic respiratory disease. Within the broader RSV-possible cohort, overall mortality was higher across every stratum, reaching an all-cause case fatality rate of 37.9 percent and an RSV-related fatality rate of 20.6 percent among patients aged 75 years and older, while remaining comparatively lower in the younger group. The study authors contextualized these descriptive observations by noting several methodological strengths alongside necessary clinical limitations. Utilizing comprehensive, nationally representative CPRD Aurum and linked HES data across five full seasons provided exceptional population breadth and minimized the impact of single-year epidemiological anomalies. However, the authors emphasized that the study design was purely descriptive without formal hypothesis testing or multivariable confounding adjustment, meaning observed numerical differences cannot be interpreted as comparative causal effects. Additionally, RSV-specific cases represented less than one percent of total episodes due to restricted historical testing practices, secondary care inpatient medication data could not be captured, and selective triage practices in intensive care units may partially explain why frailer patients aged 75 and older experienced lower critical care admission rates. Nonetheless, the substantial healthcare resource burden identified among comorbid adults aged 60 to 74 underscores the importance of evaluating targeted preventative immunization strategies for these high-risk clinical populations. supplementary_news.content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape Medical NewsMedBrief Medbrief Most Children Admitted to the ICU for Severe RSV Have No Preexisting Conditions November 23, 2026 0 Add to Email Alerts TOPLINE Among children aged 8-23 months admitted to the pediatric ICU for severe respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in their second season, about 62% had no preexisting conditions, while only about 8% met the 2023 US eligibility criteria for nirsevimab. Children who met the eligibility criteria were most likely to need invasive mechanical ventilation (40.4%). METHODOLOGY Researchers conducted a multicenter cohort study using data from the CDC's Overcoming RSV network during the 2023-2024 and 2024-2025 RSV seasons. They analyzed 574 children aged 8-23 months (median age, 1.2 years) who were admitted for at least 24 hours to the pediatric ICU at 30 pediatric hospitals in 25 states. All children had a positive result on RSV tests performed on samples obtained from the respiratory tract and had received high-flow nasal cannula therapy, noninvasive ventilation, and/or invasive mechanical ventilation. Preexisting conditions were abstracted from electronic medical records, and children were assigned hierarchically to four mutually exclusive groups: met the 2023 US nirsevimab criteria for the second season, had other identified RSV risk conditions, had other preexisting conditions, or had no preexisting conditions. Researchers compared demographic characteristics and the highest level of respiratory support received across groups. Data on nirsevimab receipt were collected only in the 2024-2025 season (n = 298). TAKEAWAY Of 574 children, 47 (8.2%) met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria, 76 (13.2%) had other identified RSV risk conditions, 96 (16.7%) had other preexisting conditions, and 355 (61.8%) had no preexisting conditions. Among children who met the eligibility criteria, 34 (72.3%) had chronic lung disease that required medical support within 6 months before the RSV season. The need for invasive mechanical ventilation rose significantly with the level of preexisting conditions: 5.9% among children with no preexisting conditions, 10.4% among those with other preexisting conditions, 17.1% among those with other identified RSV risk conditions, and 40.4% among those who met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria (P for trend < .001). Children who met the eligibility criteria or had other identified RSV risk conditions had a median hospital stay of 8.5 days compared with 5.0 days among those in the other two groups (P < .001). They also more often needed vasoactive infusions (17.0% and 13.2% vs 6.3% and 2.5%). Among 298 children admitted in the 2024-2025 season, eight (2.7%) received nirsevimab; five did not meet the eligibility criteria, and four of these five children had other identified RSV risk conditions. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was used in two children, both with other preexisting conditions; three children died (one met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria and two had other identified RSV risk conditions). IN PRACTICE "Although these findings are not population-level results and cannot ascribe risk, they could inform potential considerations for expanding nirsevimab immunization eligibility to more high-risk children in their second RSV season in the US," the authors of the study wrote. SOURCE The study was led by Regina M. Simeone, PhD, and Laura D. Zambrano, PhD, Coronavirus and Other Respiratory Viruses Division, National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, US CDC in Atlanta. It was published online on November 19, 2026, in JAMA Network Open. LIMITATIONS The sample size was small, which precluded statistical comparisons between groups and adjustment for confounders. Preexisting conditions may have been misclassified and the severity of conditions, including whether cardiac disease was hemodynamically significant, could not be assessed. Prematurity data were collected only for children younger than 12 months, and nirsevimab receipt-related data were recorded only in the second RSV season. DISCLOSURES The study was funded by a CDC contract to Boston Children's Hospital. Zambrano declared serving as a CDC employee during the conduct of this study and is now employed by Pfizer. Several authors reported receiving CDC grants during the study. Others disclosed receiving grants or fees from the National Institutes of Health, Sanofi, Pfizer, Moderna, Bavarian Nordic, and other organizations outside the submitted work. Additional author disclosures are reported in the original article. SUGGESTED FOR YOU This article was created using several editorial tools, including AI, as part of the process. Human editors reviewed this content before publication.
